chunks.content: Central Message The ages of the patients who undergo CABG in this population have changed from children to young adults. Although the preoperative left ventricular function affected the long-term outcome, the operative results were good. Perspective Most patients who had undergone CABG had multiple vessel disease due to KD. Progression of disease in nongrafted native coronary arteries and the long-term patency of the grafts require careful management for atherosclerosis with aging. Good coronary revascularization would prevent death and improves the quality of life for many years. A half-century since the first report of Kawasaki disease (KD) has passed, and the number of patients with acute KD has gradually increased with the economic development of the world. National surveys of KD in Japan have been performed every 2 years since 1976. Recently, approximately 15,000 patients with KD have been reported each year. However, the incidence of coronary artery aneurysms at 1 month after acute KD has decreased from 20% to 2% along with better awareness, diagnoses, and aggressive treatment including massive intravenous immunoglobulins since the 1990s. Therefore, the number of patients with cardiac sequelae caused by KD has decreased in the last 2 decades. However, children with coronary artery lesions in the 1970s and 1980s have grown up, and they have become adults with atherosclerotic factors. Both percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) are needed in patients with severe coronary stenotic lesions caused by KD to preserve their left ventricular function. Since the 1980s, PCI has developed remarkably as the treatment of choice for ischemic heart disease, and it has been indispensable. Recently, PCI for acute coronary syndrome in this population has often been performed. , The previous results of CABG after KD in the nationwide survey of Japan were reported in 2004. Two decades later, it is important to know how the national results of those patients who underwent CABG for coronary arterial lesions due to KD have changed. This is the first report about CABG in this population from the national database in Japan. Approximately 50 years after the first report of KD and CABG in this population, knowledge about the background characteristics and outcomes of patients who underwent CABG after KD is useful for the long-term management of patients with severe coronary stenotic lesions due to KD in the future. Material and Methods The purpose of the study was to determine the prevalence, characteristics, and outcomes of CABG for coronary artery stenosis due to KD in Japanese patients after the previous nationwide survey in 2004. The data of the patients who had undergone CABG consistent with the special criteria of KD in the Japan Cardiovascular Surgery Database (JCVSD)/National Clinical Database of Japan between 2008 and 2019 were extracted (JCVSD, Ver. 4 2008-2012, Ver. 5 2013-2019). The prevalence, background characteristics, and operative results of those patients who had undergone CABG were investigated based on the variables in the JCVSD entry form. The factors that affected the patient's condition at discharge were investigated. Furthermore, the outcomes of the patients after discharge were surveyed by questionnaires about cardiac events (CEs) after discharge between June and December in 2021. Survivals, CE-free survivals, and repeat coronary revascularization were analyzed. The survivals based on the preoperative left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) were also calculated. The Institutional Review Board number was 2020-2-9 in Shikoku Central Hospital of the Mutual Aid Association of Public School Teacher. Data Analysis The results are shown as medians with the 5th-95th percentiles and the mean ± SD values, as appropriate. A Spearman's correlation coefficient was used to examine the correlations of the rank data, such as that between the number of atherosclerotic risk factors and the age at the time of the CABG. The survival, CE-free survival, and repeat coronary revascularizations with a 95% CI were analyzed by the Kaplan–Meier method, and the differences were assessed by a log-rank test. Results Number and Age of Patients The total number of isolated CABG procedures for ischemic heart disease between 2008 and 2019 was 175,385, and the number of CABG procedures for KD was 343 (0.2%). The number of CABG procedures per year since 2008 is shown in . Recently, it has been approximately 40 patients per year. In total, 343 patients were reported by 161 (27.0%) of 596 institutions in Japan. The numbers of reported patients by the institutions were as follows: less than 5 patients, 155 institutions: 5 patients or more but less than 10 patients, 4 institutions, and 10 patients or more, 2 institutions. An elective CABG was performed in 306 patients (89.2%), and an emergency CABG was performed in 37 patients (10.8%) ( ). There were 264 male patients (77.0%) and 79 female patients (23.0%) ( , left ). In total, 343 patients were reported by 161 (27.0%) of 596 institutions in Japan. The numbers of reported patients by the institutions were as follows: less than 5 patients, 155 institutions: 5 patients or more but less than 10 patients, 4 institutions, and 10 patients or more, 2 institutions. An elective CABG was performed in 306 patients (89.2%), and an emergency CABG was performed in 37 patients (10.8%) ( ). There were 264 male patients (77.0%) and 79 female patients (23.0%) ( , left ). The median age at the time of the CABG was 39 years (5th-95th percentile, 13-72). There were 39 patients (11%) aged less than 20 years and 258 adult patients (75.2%) aged 20 to 60 years. For CABG, there were 10 mitral valve surgeries (2.6%) and 9 aortic valve surgeries (2.9%). A left ventriculoplasty for ventricular aneurysms was performed in 6 patients (1.7%)—septal anterior ventricular exclusion in 3, Dor procedure in 2, and myotomy in 1. Background Characteristics of Patient Population Preoperative condition Cardiogenic shock was found in 10 patients (2.9%), and consciousness disturbance within 24 hours was present in 4 patients (1.1%) ( ). Acute myocardial infarctions (AMIs) before the CABG were found in 64 patients (18.6%). The interval from the AMI to the CABG was less than 24 hours in 14 patients and 1 day or more but less than 21 days in 15 patients. Heart failure was found in 60 patients (17.5%). PCIs before the CABG were performed in 50 patients (14.6%). Stable angina and unstable angina were found in 174 patients (50.7%) and 52 patients (15.2%), respectively. The LVEF by any method was preserved (≥60%) in 187 patients (54.6%), intermediate (≥30% but <60%) in 134 patients (39.0%), and poor (<30%) in 22 patients (6.4%). History and surgery Sixteen patients (5.0%) had undergone a previous CABG, and 1 patient had undergone a valve surgery. Systemic arterial lesions other than coronary artery disease were found in 19 patients (5.5%). Arrhythmias were present in 21 patients (6.1%), including sustained ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation in 13 patients (3.8%), atrial tachycardia or atrial fibrillation in 6 patients (1.8%), and others in 2 patients (0.6%). Atherosclerotic risk factors The median height was 167 cm (5 th -95 th percentile, 148-180), and median weight was 64 kg (42-90.7). The median body mass index was 22.9 kg/m 2 (17.2-30.9). A total of 124 patients (36.2%) had a history of smoking, and 43 patients (12.5%) were current smokers. The numbers with each risk factor were as follows: dyslipidemia, 126 patients (36.7%); hypertension, 109 patients (31.8%); body mass index more than 26 kg/m 2 , 75 patients (21.9%); diabetes mellitus, 35 patients (10.2%). The number of these 4 risk factors per patient was as follows: none, 157 patients (45.7%); 1, 76 patients (22.2%); 2, 72 patients (21.0%); 3, 27 patients (7.9%); and 4, 11 patients (3.2%). Between the number of risk factors and age at CABG, the correlation coefficient was 0.493 ( P < .0001) ( , right ). Operation Coronary artery bypass grafting Among 640 grafts in the 343 patients undergoing CABG, the vessel conduits were the left internal thoracic artery in 277 (43.3%); right internal thoracic artery in 106 (16.6%); saphenous vein in 154 (24.1%); gastroepiploic artery in 49 (7.7%); radial artery in 53 (8.3%); and other in 1. The number of internal thoracic arteries was as follows: none in 22 patients (6.4%); 1 in 136 patients (40.0%), 2 in 99 patients (28.9%), and not written for 86 patients (24.7%). The mean number of grafts was 2.3 ± 1.1 per patient. The target coronary arteries were the left anterior descending artery in 311 patients (38.5%); right coronary artery in 235 patients (29.2%); left circumflex (posterolateral artery, posterior descending, obtuse marginal artery) in 183 patients (22.7%); and diagonal branch in 77 patients (9.6%). Valve surgery with coronary artery bypass grafting Seven patients underwent mitral valvuloplasty, and 3 patients underwent mitral valve replacement. The median age of the patients who underwent mitral valve surgery was 49 years (range, 16-70). LVEF ranged from 20% to 60%, with a median of 35%. The etiologies of the mitral valve dysfunction were degenerative changes in 6 patients and ischemic changes in 2 patients. Seven patients underwent aortic valve replacement, and 2 patients underwent aortic valvuloplasty. The median age of the patients who underwent aortic valve surgery was 65 years (25-76). LVEF ranged from 32% to 70%, with a median of 57%. The etiologies of the aortic valve dysfunction were degenerative changes with aging in 7 patients, an infective change in 1 patient, and other in 1 patient. Operative Data, Reoperation, and Complication Off-pump CABG and on-pump CABG were performed in 144 patients (42.0%) and 199 patients (58.0%), respectively. The median age of patients who underwent off-pump CABG was 37.5 years (5th-95th percentile, 13-72) and of patients who underwent on-pump CABG was 41 years (12-73). There was no difference between the 2 groups ( P = .067). The number of patients who underwent off-pump CABG depending on left ventricular function, that is, preserved, intermediate, and poor, was 87 (46%), 52 (39%), and 5 (22%), respectively. The mean operative time was 334 ± 139 minutes ( ). The mean admission duration was 23 ± 16 days. The mean intensive care unit stay was 3 ± 5 days, and the mean postoperative hospital stay was 17 ± 14 days. Assisted circulation was applied as follows: intra-aortic balloon pump preoperatively in 33 patients (9.6%) and percutaneous cardiopulmonary support preoperatively in 4 patients (1.2%). Allogeneic transfusions and autotransfusions were performed in 127 patients (37%) and 38 patients (11%), respectively. Nineteen (5.5%) of 343 patients underwent a reoperation. Complications occurred in 73 patients (21.8%). Treatment at Discharge Antiplatelet agents after CABG were administered to 343 patients; 318 (92.7%) received aspirin, and 48 (14.0%) received other antiplatelet agents. Warfarin was given to 133 patients (38.8%) patients, and non–vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants were administered to 4 patients. The medications used were beta-blockers in 198 patients (57.8%); calcium antagonists in 87 patients (25.4%); angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors in 24 patients (7.0%); angiotensin receptor blockers in 24 patients (7.0%); antiarrhythmic agents in 20 patients (5.8%); and statins in 143 patients (41.7%). Death and General Condition at Discharge Three of the 343 patients died, and the 30-day-operative mortality was 0.9%. The causes of death were hemorrhage in 1 patient, low output syndrome in 1 patient, and other in 1 patient. The patients’ general conditions at discharge were as follows: unaffected (modified Rankin scale 0-3) in 328 patients (95.6%); moderately compromised (modified Rankin scale 4) in 8 patients (2.3%); and severely compromised (modified Rankin scale 5) in 4 patients (1.2%). Twelve patients (3.5%) were readmitted within 30 days after discharge. The causes of the readmissions were arrhythmias in 2 patients, chronic heart failure in 2 patients, an incision complication in 1 patient, pericardial effusion/tamponade in 1 patient, pneumonia in 1 patient, and others in 5 patients. Risk Factors for Compromised General Condition at Discharge After Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting The rate of each factor in the 2 groups based on the general condition at discharge after CABG is shown in . One was the unaffected patient group (n = 328), and the other was the affected patient group, which included compromised patients at discharge and deaths (n = 15). A patient with a modified Rankin scale more than 3 was classified in the compromised patient group. Risk factors related to a poor general condition at discharge were age at operation, AMI, heart failure, cardiogenic shock, additional cardiac mechanical support, history of an arrhythmia, preoperative LVEF, New York Heart Association class III or greater, emergency operation, reoperation, and complications. Postoperative Clinical Status From the Questionnaires Information after discharge from the questionnaires was obtained for 183 patients (53.8%) ( ). Of the 183 patients, 176 survived (96.2%) and 7 died (3.8%). The causes of late deaths were cardiac in 2 patients, noncardiac in 4 patients, and unknown in 1 patient. Follow-up was available for 108 patients (58.1%), 20 patients (10.8%) dropped out, and 52 patients (28.0%) were transferred to another institution. Twenty-six patients (14.0%) had symptoms (angina in 8, palpitations in 7, exertional dyspnea in 3, and others in 8). CEs occurred in 14 patients (7.5%) (AMI in 4, syncope in 2, heart failure in 2, and others in 6). Repeat coronary revascularization involved CABG in 15 patients (8.1%) and PCI in 11 patients (5.4%). An implantable cardioverter defibrillator and a cardiac resynchronization-defibrillator were implanted in 1 patient each. The median value of the postoperative LVEF was 61% (5th-95th percentile, 37-75) (n = 169). Survival and Cardiac Event–Free Survival The survivals after CABG at 1, 5, and 10 years were 99% (95% CI, 95-99), 96% (95% CI, 89-98), and 94% (95% CI, 87-97), respectively (n = 183) ( , left ). Based on the age at CABG, the survival for the group aged less than 40 years of age at 10 years was 97% (95% CI, 90-99) (n = 100), and the corresponding value for the group aged 40 years or more was 90% (95% CI, 74-96) (n = 83) ( , left upper ). There was no difference between the 2 groups ( P = .39). Based on off-pump CABG, the survival for the off-pump group at 10 years was 96% (95% CI, 84-99) (n = 91), and the corresponding value for the on-pump group was 92% (80-97) (n = 91) ( , right upper ). There was no difference between the 2 groups ( P = .36). The 5-year survivals according to the preoperative LVEF were 72% (13--96) (n = 9) for the poor group, 98% (87-100) (n = 104) for the preserved group, and 94% (81-98) (n = 70) for the intermediate group. The number of deaths in the preserved, intermediate, and poor groups was 1 (1%), 5 (6.6%), and 1 (11%), respectively ( ). The survival was significantly lower in the poor group than in the preserved groups ( P = .008). The CE-free survivals after CABG at 1, 5, and 10 years were 98% (94-99), 89% (82-93), and 75% (56-87), respectively (n = 183) ( , left lower ). The repeat coronary revascularization–free rates at 1, 5, and 10 years after CABG were 92% (87-95), 88% (82-92), and 74% (56-86), respectively (n = 183) ( , right lower ). The overall CE-free survivals including for repeat coronary revascularization after CABG at 1, 5, and 10 years were 91% (86-94), 82% (74-87), and 66% (49-78), respectively (n = 183) ( , right ). Discussion CABG after KD has been performed recently in approximately 40 patients per year. The prevalence of CABG from the annual incidence of KD in Japan is approximately 0.3%. The present results were compared with the nationwide survey of 2004 ( ). The median age of the patients with CABG was more in the present study than the 11.8 years in the national survey of 2004. The number of patients who had undergone CABG at less than 20 years of age was only 11% in this study. The number of children who needed CABG had decreased, and most of the patients were adults who had acute KD in the 1980s. The results were caused by a decrease in coronary artery aneurysms and AMIs in children with antithrombotic therapy for patients with giant aneurysms immediately after acute KD. Children with severe coronary artery lesions had undergone CABG before the previous 3 decades. However, the data reflected the fact that CABG could be given more consideration in adult patients years later. It was found that coronary artery lesions progressed in adults, and CEs also occurred many years after the onset of KD. , , Although the largest number of patients had an age at onset of acute KD of approximately 1 year, the age at the time of the operation and the interval from the onset of KD to the operation varied. The degree of progression of coronary stenotic lesions after KD varies, and the rate in each branch differs in each patient. The difficulty of the surgical timing depends on the characteristics of the coronary artery lesions due to KD. , The number of elective CABG procedures was greater in this population. However, an emergency CABG is often needed in some patients with KD and AMIs. A Japanese survey of AMIs in adult patients with coronary artery lesions caused by KD from 2012 to 2019 has been reported. In that report, 73 patients had AMI-KD, and included 0.1% of the patients with AMI and no KD. The median age of the patients with AMI-KD was 35 years, and the patients with AMI without KD were significantly younger. PCI was performed in 53.2% of the patients with AMI-KD, and primary stent implantations were performed in 21.9%. Compared with the AMI non-KD group, the AMI-KD group underwent non-PCI strategies such as CABG or thrombolysis, and they required intensive therapy with mechanical supports more often. Fourteen percent of the patients with AMI-KD had undergone CABG in the registry. The percentage of emergency CABG was only 10% in this survey, and it is the corresponding value. Compared with the AMI non-KD group, the AMI-KD group underwent non-PCI strategies such as CABG or thrombolysis, and they required intensive therapy with mechanical supports more often. Fourteen percent of the patients with AMI-KD had undergone CABG in the registry. The percentage of emergency CABG was only 10% in this survey, and it is the corresponding value. In the present study, the number of operative deaths was low. The factors related to compromised condition at discharge were AMI, heart failure, and cardiogenic shock before the operation, and cardiac mechanical support. Those factors are related to LVEF, and they may be significant for an emergency CABG. It seems that the elective operative results are better than the emergency operative results from the present study. An elective CABG would be appropriate for multiple stenotic coronary artery lesions to avoid an emergency CABG if there is an indication for coronary revascularization. The number of mean grafts in the present results increased compared with the previous results. In the late period after acute KD, many patients with giant aneurysms often had segmental stenosis, which reflects recanalization after a thrombotic occlusion. Localized stenosis in adults progresses slowly for years. It was considered that the number of used grafts and stenotic lesions in adults was more than in children. In the target vessels, the number of left circumflex arteries in adults increased compared with children. Two-thirds of the patients in the present study underwent CABG with internal thoracic artery grafts. The results are similar to the previous results. The number of radial artery grafts in the present results increased, and they were useful in adult patients ( ). When the number and length of grafts are limited, sequential grafting and a combination graft of the internal thoracic artery and the radial artery are used for revascularization of multiple-vessel disease or reoperations in adults. The number of off-pump CABG operations was increased in the present study. It is useful in adult patients with low left ventricular function because it decreases the surgical invasiveness of the operation. The postoperative condition of patients surviving CABG is good. , , Progression of the disease in nongrafted native coronary arteries and the long-term patency of the grafts require careful management for atherosclerosis with aging. Repeat coronary revascularization in 10% to 20% of the patients may be needed at 10 years after the CABG. Catheter intervention for native coronary arteries has recently improved with the development of drug-eluting stents. Antithrombotic therapy after CABG was given to all surviving patients, and warfarin was given to approximately 30% of the patients in this survey. Warfarin may be useful in adult patients with giant aneurysms in nongrafted arteries, not only in children with giant aneurysms immediately after acute KD. Furthermore, non–vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants may be considered in this population. Approximately one-third of patients had risk factors. Patients with multiple risk factors were older than patients without risk factors, suggesting that the prevalence of each atherosclerotic risk factor increased with age. The occurrence of acute coronary syndrome can cause atherosclerotic factors in addition to coronary artery lesions caused by KD. Even if some patients with coronary artery lesions caused by KD are asymptomatic as children, they become symptomatic with aging. Therefore, CABG is needed in adult patients with multiple coronary artery stenosis as coronary revascularization. Furthermore, medications may be required for the treatment of cardiac failure, protection from atherosclerosis and myocardial damage, and treatment of arrhythmias. The prognosis after CABG depended on the LVEF, and it was poor in patients with a decreased LVEF. Device implantations for fatal arrhythmias and poor left ventricular function would be needed in patients with low LVEF. Left ventriculoplasty may be useful in some patients. Study Limitations We did not perform a multivariate analysis of the affected factors on the condition at discharge because the number of the affected patient conditions was small. Information after discharge from questionnaires was obtained from approximately 50%, and the information after discharge was limited. It is possible that some patients whose history of KD had not been confirmed in the acute phase might have been included in the patients aged more than 60 years at the operation because KD was first reported in 1967. In this study, it was lack in information for the completeness of revascularization in each patient. It is important that the graft patency rate is studied, and for that, more long-term investigation is needed. Introduction Highlights What is already known Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is associated with improved clinical outcomes in patients at high surgical risk when compared with surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR). New trials have shown that TAVR is noninferior to SAVR in patients at low to intermediate surgical risk at 1 year of follow-up. However, data about long-term safety and efficacy is limited. What this study adds A longitudinal comparison of TAVR versus SAVR demonstrated a comparable risk of all-cause death at 30 days, 1 year, and 2 years of follow-up. However, at 5 years or longer follow-up TAVR was associated with an increased risk of all-cause death. While TAVR showed certain procedural advantages, the choice between TAVR and SAVR in patients with low or intermediate surgical risk should consider long-term outcomes, with SAVR potentially being more favorable due to better survival observed on longer follow-up durations. Aortic stenosis (AS) is one of the most prevalent forms of valvular heart disease in the senior population . The frequency of severe, potentially fatal AS will rise as the population ages . With a 12.4% incidence of AS in North America and Europe, it may be inferred that over 291 000 candidates have received aortic valve replacements . It has been demonstrated that people with AS have reduced cardiac outflow, which raises cardiac workload and leads to heart failure and left ventricular hypertrophy. A prior study found that individuals with symptoms of AS, such as angina, syncope, or heart failure, experienced yearly death rates of close to 25% . Therefore, individuals with AS require efficient treatment options. Surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) is the present treatment protocol for severe symptomatic AS . However, it has been demonstrated that individuals with calcified aortas, scars from prior cardiac surgeries, or advanced age are at a higher risk for SAVR. This increased risk in the patients is due to inherent challenges in surgery, such as the need to address adhesions, extended procedure times, and complications related to clamping, rather than indicating a decrease in the effectiveness of valve replacement. Hence, there have been significant advancements in therapy alternatives. Many studies – have shown transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) as a novel alternative strategy for inoperable or high surgical-risk AS patients due to its less invasive nature , . However, it is unclear if these findings apply to AS patients with low to intermediate surgical risk too. Two recent trials DEDICATE (Randomized, Multicenter, Event-Driven Trial of TAVR vs. SAVR in Patients with Symptomatic Severe Aortic-Valve Stenosis) and NOTION-2 (Nordic Aortic Valve Intervention), have shown conflicting outcomes among patients with low or intermediate surgical risk undergoing TAVR versus SAVR , . Although the DEDICATE trial showed a significant reduction in all-cause death with TAVR at 1 year of follow-up , the NOTION-2 trial showed a comparable rate of all-cause death and the composite endpoint (all-cause death, stroke, and rehospitalization) at 1 year of follow-up with TAVR versus SAVR . These conflicted findings warrant the need for a meta-analysis to comprehensively synthesize the available evidence regarding not only the comparative efficacy but also the long-term outcomes of TAVR versus SAVR in patients with severe AS at low or intermediate surgical risk. While short-term outcomes have been evaluated extensively, there is a lack of consolidated data addressing the differences between the two groups over extended follow-up periods. Moreover, a comparison between the two treatment options at various time intervals has yet to be conducted. To bridge this literature gap and to determine the most optimal course of treatment in this patient subset, we conducted a meta-analysis comparing the two treatment options. Methods This systematic review and meta-analysis has been reported in concordance with guidelines provided by preferred reporting items for systematic review and meta-analyses (PRISMA, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/D564 ) . Approval from the institutional review board was not required since the included studies were publicly available with patient information de-identified. Data sources and search strategy An electronic search of Cochrane Library, PubMed/MEDLINE, and Embase was conducted for relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and their follow-up reports, that aimed to assess the safety and efficacy of SAVR compared with TAVR in patients with low surgical risk from their inception through 10th May 2024, without any time or language restrictions. Medical subject headings (MESH) terms along with Boolean operators were used to devise an effective search strategy for each database (Table S1, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/D564 ). We also performed a manual search for additional relevant studies using references of previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses to ensure no important publications were overlooked. The following predefined inclusion criteria were used: (i) RCTs; (ii) short (<1 year), intermediate (2–4 years), or long-term (≥5 years) follow-up reports of RCTs; (iii) RCTs that included adult male or female patients who were >18

inception through 10th May 2024, without any time or language restrictions. Medical subject headings (MESH) terms along with Boolean operators were used to devise an effective search strategy for each database (Table S1, Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/D564 ). We also performed a manual search for additional relevant studies using references of previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses to ensure no important publications were overlooked. The following predefined inclusion criteria were used: (i) RCTs; (ii) short (<1 year), intermediate (2–4 years), or long-term (≥5 years) follow-up reports of RCTs; (iii) RCTs that included adult male or female patients who were >18 years old; (iv) patients with severe AS, classified as having a low or intermediate surgical risk; (v) compared clinical outcomes of SAVR with TAVR; and (vi) assessed at least one of the predetermined clinical outcomes. Low surgical risk was defined as a mean STS score of <4% and/or a logistic EuroSCORE of <10%. Intermediate surgical risk was defined as a mean STS score of 4–8% and/or a logistic EuroSCORE of 10–20%. In the case of trials reporting outcomes at two different intervals for the same follow-up strata (e.g. for long-term follow-up, if outcomes were separately reported for 5 and 6-year follow-up, the data was extracted and pooled for longer follow-up). Post-hoc analyses of parent RCTs were excluded. The detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria of our meta-analysis are given in Table S2 (Supplemental Digital Content 1, http://links.lww.com/JS9/D564 ). Study selection All articles retrieved from the systematic search were exported to EndNote Reference Manager (Version X7.5; Clarivate Analytics, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, 2016) where duplicates were sought and removed. The remaining articles were then assessed at the title and abstract level by two independent investigators (A.A. and F.A.), after which full texts were read to confirm relevance. Any disagreements were resolved by mutual discussion with a third investigator (M.A.). Data extraction, outcomes, and quality assessment Two investigators (A.A. and Z.A.N.) autonomously extracted data from the selected studies on prespecified collection forms. Data were extracted, including trial name, publication year, number of patients in TAVR and SAVR groups, mean age of patients, percentage of males among the study participants, details of the patient population, STS score, intervention subtype, duration of follow-up, and outcome measures. The primary outcomes included all-cause death and cardiac death. The secondary outcomes included; myocardial infarction (MI), transient ischemic attack (TIA), stroke, valve endocarditis, prosthetic-valve thrombosis, permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI), acute kidney injury, new-onset or worsening atrial fibrillation (AF), which was defined as an increase in the severity, frequency, or duration of AF episodes, new-onset left bundle-branch block, major vascular complications, major bleeding, hospitalization, coronary obstruction, cardiogenic shock and aortic-valve reintervention. All outcomes except periprocedural were assessed on short (<1 year), intermediate (2–5 years), and long-term (≥5 years) follow-ups. A similar methodology has been used in prior studies – . To assess the quality of included RCTs, we used the Cochrane risk of bias tool (RoB 2.0) . The risk of bias was assessed across the following domains: randomization, deviations from intended variation, missing outcome data, measurement of outcome, and selection of reported results. The trials were scored based on a high, some concerns, or low risk of bias in each domain. Traffic light plots were created using the Robvis tool . Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was performed by pooling RR with corresponding 95% CIs for each clinical outcome. Data was pooled using the random-effects model in the R version 4.4.1. Forest plots were created to visualize the results of pooling. Heterogeneity across studies was evaluated using Higgins I 2 , and a value of I 2 =25–50% was considered mild, 50–75% as moderate, and I 2 >75% as severe . The total number of included studies was less than 10; hence, the publication bias could not be assessed using funnel plots. A P -value <0.05 was considered statistically significant in all cases. Results A systematic literature search of databases/registers identified 3350 records. The duplicate studies were removed and 2285 articles were screened based on their titles and abstracts by two independent investigators. This process identified 2175 articles that were excluded and full texts of 110 articles were retrieved for screening. The review of full texts determined 17 reports that met our prespecified inclusion criteria. Results of the meta-analysis Primary outcomes All-cause death: No significant association was observed of all-cause death with TAVR or SAVR at 30 days (RR: 0.94, 95% CI: 0.61–1.45, I 2 =15%, seven studies), at 1 year (RR: 0.78, 95% CI: 0.61–1.01, I 2 =42%, eight studies), and at 2 years (RR: 0.97, 95% CI: 0.84–1.12, I 2 =0%, five studies). Discussion In this systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 reports and 9092 individuals, we sought to compare TAVR with SAVR in patients with AS who are at low to intermediate surgical risk. This comparison is significant because, while TAVR has become increasingly popular in high-risk patients due to its minimally invasive nature, its role in patients with low to intermediate surgical risk remains debated, with concerns about long-term efficacy, safety, and durability compared to SAVR. Our pooled analysis demonstrated no statistically significant difference between TAVR and SAVR for reducing all-cause death at 30 days, 1 year, and 2 years but significantly increased risk with TAVR at 5 years or longer follow-up. TAVR was associated with a significantly decreased risk for cardiac death at 1-year follow-up and comparable risk at 30 days, 2 years, and 5 years or longer follow-up. TAVR showed a significantly lower risk of major bleeding events at 30 days; however, it was associated with a significantly increased risk of major vascular complications at 30 days and PPI at 30 days, 1 year, and at 2 years; lower risk of AKI at 30 days and 1 year and lower risk of new onset or worsening AF at 30 days, 1 year, and 2 years when compared with SAVR. TAVR was also associated with a significantly reduced risk of cardiogenic shock at 30 days. No statistically significant difference was observed between TAVR and SAVR in reducing the risk of MI, stroke, valve endocarditis, risk of hospitalizations, and TIAs. However, TAVR was associated with a significantly increased risk of TIA at 2 years, and an increased risk of new-onset left bundle-branch block at 1 year. TAVR was also associated with a significantly increased risk of prosthetic valve thrombosis at 2 years and aortic-valve reintervention at 1 year follow-up. Although previous meta-analyses have been conducted on this topic , , our study offers new insights. We pooled clinical outcomes at short to long-term follow-ups, providing a better insight regarding the clinical effectiveness of TAVR versus SAVR. Our analysis revealed no statistically significant difference between TAVR and SAVR in reducing all-cause mortality at 30 days, 1 year, and 2 years. This result is consistent with several other studies , that showed TAVR to be noninferior to SAVR. However, after 5 years or longer follow-up, our analysis found a significantly elevated risk linked to TAVR. Several factors should be considered while interpreting the increased risk of all-cause death with TAVR at 5 years or longer follow-up. NOTION trial investigators reported the longest follow-up data in our pooled analysis for TAVR versus SAVR . In this study, all consecutive patients were eligible for enrollment in the trial without determining a specific risk profile. As a result, the investigators included a large number of older patients with a mean age of 79 years, although they were predominantly low-risk individuals. Over 80% of the included patients had an STS-PROM score of less than 4% and limited comorbidities. An observational study reported all-cause death rates of 7.1% at 5 years of follow-up and 12.4% at 8 years following isolated SAVR . In contrast, the NOTION trial had all-cause death rates of 28.9 and 52.6% at 5 and 8 years of follow-up , . After 10 years of follow-up, around 60% of the patients had died, which indicated a higher risk profile of included patients than that determined solely based on STS-PROM score . In the PARTNER 3 trial, which included younger patients (mean age 73 years) at low surgical risk, the 5-year all-cause mortality rates were 10.0% for TAVR and 8.2% for SAVR . In the PARTNER 2 trial, which included patients at intermediate surgical risk with a mean age of 81.6 years, all-cause death rates at 5 years were 46.0% in the TAVR group and 42.1% in the SAVR group . PARTNER 3 trial, which included younger patients (mean age 73 years) at low surgical risk, the 5-year all-cause mortality rates were 10.0% for TAVR and 8.2% for SAVR . In the PARTNER 2 trial, which included patients at intermediate surgical risk with a mean age of 81.6 years, all-cause death rates at 5 years were 46.0% in the TAVR group and 42.1% in the SAVR group . It is important to mention that SAPIEN XT was employed in the PARTNER 2 trial which is no longer in clinical use in the USA and has been largely replaced by more advanced generations like the SAPIEN 3 valve. While the second-generation valve, SAPIEN XT, demonstrated procedural success, it was associated with higher rates of paravalvular leakage and aortic regurgitation, which has been linked to poorer long-term outcomes, including increased mortality . The newer valves have significantly improved upon these outcomes , . TAVR was linked to a notably decreased risk of cardiac mortality at 1 year, indicating a possible early benefit concerning outcomes specific to the heart. Nevertheless, this advantage was not sustained over a year, as TAVR and SAVR had similar risks of cardiac mortality after 30 days, 2 years, and 5 years or more. The reduction in cardiac death at 1 year may reflect a statistical anomaly rather than a true clinical effect, given the difference was not consistent across other time points of 30 days, 2 years, or 5 years. Our findings highlight the need for long-term follow-up studies for TAVR to compare its durability with SAVR, especially as long-term data for SAVR is widely available. A significant challenge in evaluating TAVR outcomes is the regular introduction of new TAVR valve generations. Although long-term data on TAVR exists, they are based on previous generations of valves and are therefore considered outdated due to the advancement in valve designs. Compared to SAVR, TAVR showed a significantly decreased risk of major bleeding episodes at 30 days. This is likely because TAVR is a less invasive procedure that induces less surgical stress and requires minimal anticoagulant medication . Additionally, at 30 days, 1 year, and 2 years, TAVR was linked to a decreased risk of AKI as well as a lower risk of new-onset or worsening AF. The potential correlation between the lower risk of AKI and TAVR might be attributed to two factors: the TAVR procedure’s less invasive nature and its ability to prevent cardiopulmonary bypass . The association of TAVR with a lower risk of new-onset or worsening AF is likely due to its less invasive nature, which reduces surgical trauma, oxidative stress, inflammation, and the overall hemodynamic burden of surgery . These results demonstrate the procedural benefits of TAVR, especially concerning lowering perioperative and early postoperative complications. The reduced incidence of cardiogenic shock with TAVR could be due to the procedure’s ability to minimize cardiac stress and preserve hemodynamic stability in the immediate postoperative period attributed to the less intrusive technique . Conversely, TAVR was associated with an increased risk of major vascular complications. This can be linked to the transcatheter procedure, which involves navigating the vascular system, thereby increasing the likelihood of vascular injuries . The transcatheter valve’s location, which may interfere with the heart’s electrical conduction system , might explain the higher risk of permanent pacemaker placement with TAVR observed in our study , . Moreover, the preexisting right bundle branch block and new-onset left bundle branch block, coupled with the older age of patients, are key factors contributing to the increased risk of pacemaker implantation after TAVR . The risk of MI, stroke, hospitalizations, and TIAs was comparable between TAVR and SAVR across all time points. Our analysis demonstrated no significant differences between the two groups in the risk of prosthetic valve thrombosis at 30 days, 1 year, or 5 years. However, at 2 years, TAVR was associated with a significantly increased risk of prosthetic valve thrombosis. Thrombosis was typically diagnosed through imaging and echocardiographic findings, and although most trials reported the use of antithrombotic or anticoagulant therapy, details regarding whether it led to reintervention were not consistently reported. Similarly, no significant differences were observed in aortic-valve reintervention rates at 30 days, 2 years, or 5 years, but TAVR showed a significantly increased risk at 1 year. Further details regarding reintervention, including whether TAVR explanation was required, were not provided. Several factors, such as valve degeneration or patient baseline characteristics could explain these findings, but further investigation is needed. This study has some limitations. Firstly, this is a study-level meta-analysis, and the absence of patient-level information made it challenging to evaluate the impact of important moderators, such as the percentage of bicuspid valves. Several factors, such as valve degeneration or patient baseline characteristics could explain these findings, but further investigation is needed. This study has some limitations. Firstly, this is a study-level meta-analysis, and the absence of patient-level information made it challenging to evaluate the impact of important moderators, such as the percentage of bicuspid valves. This limits our ability to account for variations in patient characteristics that may influence the outcomes. The effect of AKI on mortality could not be evaluated as well due to limited available data. Secondly, significant heterogeneity was observed in some of the outcomes, which could be attributed to deviations from intended interventions in pooled studies along with a considerable variability in the patients’ characteristics. The variations in the use of valve types, baseline STS scores, and age of patients could have influenced our findings. These variations may affect the generalizability of our findings to broader patient populations. The prognosis of patients with AS who are at low to intermediate surgical risk may be impacted by the lack of information on treatment regimens following TAVR or SAVR in the included trials, further limiting the applicability of our results to clinical practice. Moreover, it is important to note key criticisms of several trials comparing TAVR to SAVR. Trials comparing these patients have been criticized for including concomitant procedures in the surgical arm (such as CABG or other valve interventions), reoperations, and various valve replacement options for patients in the SAVR group, all of which increase the surgical risk and heterogeneity of the patients, compared to TAVR patients which are not impacted by these factors and receive one or two of the most advanced valve options. These confounding variables have made it very difficult to determine the differences in outcomes between patients and likely have contributed to noninferiority findings in some trials as well as conflicting findings in others. To further validate the effectiveness of TAVR compared to SAVR, future research should focus on long-term, large-scale RCTs with extended follow-up periods. Such studies should include patient-level data to account for individual variations. Moreover, ensuring more homogeneity in study populations and using standardized outcome measures will enhance the reliability of future findings. Detailed reporting of postprocedural management and treatment regimens will also be essential to gaining a better understanding of their impact on outcomes, allowing for more accurate comparisons between TAVR and SAVR. Particularly, for younger patients with a longer life expectancy, studies should address concerns about the long-term durability of TAVR valves and the elevated risks observed at extended follow-ups. The durability of TAVR valves remains an important factor in determining the optimal treatment approach for these patients, as the higher mortality and complications associated with TAVR at longer follow-up suggest SAVR may provide superior long-term advantages in this population. Understanding the economic viability of TAVR compared to SAVR will also be important as TAVR evolves and becomes more widely adopted. Conclusion Our meta-analysis concludes that, for patients with aortic stenosis at low to intermediate surgical risk, while TAVR offers significant short-term advantages over SAVR, such as reduced bleeding events, lower risks of AKI, and new-onset or worsening AF, these advantages are outweighed by its poorer long-term outcomes. Both TAVR and SAVR demonstrated comparable rates of all-cause death up to 2 years of follow-up. However, long-term outcomes reveal important drawbacks, including higher mortality with TAVR at extended follow-up periods. TAVR was also associated with significantly increased PPI and major vascular complications. Unlike previous studies, our analysis provides a comprehensive comparison of TAVR and SAVR across a wide range of time-points, highlighting these long-term differences and complications. Given these findings, SAVR can be considered a reliable treatment option for younger people with low to intermediate surgical risk, due to its more favorable medium to long-term outcomes. Future research should focus on improving the durability of TAVR valves and minimizing procedure-specific complications to enhance its long-term efficacy.
