The risk of cardiovascular events and hypertension-mediated organ damage (HMOD) is less associated with white coat hypertension. Still, it can be related to increased chances of long-term cardiovascular problems, as reported by recent studies [ , ]. Therefore, patients with whitecoat hypertension are encouraged to make necessary lifestyle modifications to reduce cardiovascular risk and undergo regular follow-up appointments with consistent out-of-office blood pressure monitoring. In addition, antihypertensive drug treatment can be considered for the whitecoat hypertensive patients with a high cardiovascular risk profile [ ]. 3. Ischemic Heart Disease Ischemic heart disease (IHD) or coronary heart disease (CHD) is a pathological condition characterized by a discrepancy between myocardial oxygen demand and supply due to reduced cardiac blood flow [ ]. Blockage of coronary arteries due to the atherosclerotic plaque is the most common cause of IHD. Other causes include coronary artery spasm, coronary arteritis, embolism or shock secondary to hypotension, etc. Due to its pathophysiology, IHD is also known as coronary artery disease (CAD). According to WHO Global Health Estimates, IHD is the leading cause of mortality globally, causing 16% of deaths alone [ ]. In addition, more than half of all the cardiovascular events in patients less than 75 years of age are due to IHD. After the age of 40, the risk for developing the IHD is 49% in males and 32% in females [ ]. IHD can be categorized as chronic coronary syndromes or acute coronary syndromes. Acute coronary syndromes (ACS) include unstable angina pectoris and acute myocardial infarction. Stable angina is one of the types of Chronic Coronary Syndromes (CCS). Dental practitioners must be well aware of the significant risk factors associated with IHD and their level of control to estimate the likelihood of the dental procedure concluding uneventfully. Some non-modifiable risk factors for IHD are age, male gender, family history, and co-morbidities like kidney disease, thyroid disease, and type I and II diabetes along with others. However, the most common and modifiable risk factors include lipid disorders, high blood pressure, smoking, alcohol, diabetes, obesity, and stress [ ]. In the early stages, the disease is generally asymptomatic. Nevertheless, as atherosclerosis worsens, symptoms appear, especially during emotional or physical stress when oxygen demand increases. Symptoms may include fatigue, shortness of breath, chest pain (angina), and ankle edema. Angina pectoris is a sudden onset, substernal pain in the chest due to myocardial ischemia without infarction or necrosis. The pain may radiate to the left arm, left jaw, neck, teeth, or back. Anginal pain radiating to the mandible can mimic the pain of dental origin. Also, the probability of an anginal attack in a dental environment rises due to anxiety, fear, and pain [ ]. Thus, a dental practitioner must be well aware of the clinical manifestations of angina and its management in the dental clinic. Angina is categorized as stable, unstable, or Prinzmetal angina. • Stable angina is precipitated by physical exertion or emotional stress and lasts for less than 15 minutes. • Unstable angina represents a more severe and longer-lasting form of angina that occurs at rest without evidence of necrosis. • Prinzmetal/variant angina occurs at rest and is most likely due to coronary artery spasm. Complete blockage of one or more coronary arteries leads to persistent ischemia and irreversible necrosis of myocardial tissues, which eventually lead to heart attack or myocardial infarction. Diagnosis of IHD includes assessment of symptoms, resting electrocardiogram (ECG), stress ECG, coronary computed tomography angiography (CTA), stress cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) perfusion imaging, positron emission tomography (PET), or single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) perfusion imaging. In addition, invasive coronary angiography (ICA) is recommended to diagnose and manage patients with a high likelihood of IHD. Treatment of IHD comprises the following: (1) Antithrombotic/antiplatelet therapy- low dose aspirin [ , ], clopidogrel [ ], ticagrelor [ ]; (2) Antianginal medication- sublingual nitroglycerin; (3) Modification of cardiovascular risk factors [ ] — reducing low-density lipoproteins (LDL), healthy diet, smoking cessation, and exercise; (4) Revascularization- percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). There is a high risk of recurrence of cardiovascular events in patients with myocardial infarction (MI). Previous AHA guidelines recommended that any dental surgery within six months of MI should be avoided due to the high risk of complications during this duration [ ]. The emerging evidence in cardiovascular disease management advocates that no elective dental care should be given within 30 days of MI. Any emergency care during this period should be given after the physician’s consultation and in a hospital-based setup. After one month, if the patient is symptom-free, elective dental care can be provided with caution [ ]. Patients with angina or

of recurrence of cardiovascular events in patients with myocardial infarction (MI). Previous AHA guidelines recommended that any dental surgery within six months of MI should be avoided due to the high risk of complications during this duration [ ]. The emerging evidence in cardiovascular disease management advocates that no elective dental care should be given within 30 days of MI. Any emergency care during this period should be given after the physician’s consultation and in a hospital-based setup. After one month, if the patient is symptom-free, elective dental care can be provided with caution [ ]. Patients with angina or a history of myocardial infarction are managed similarly in a dental setup. Though patients with unstable angina must be immediately referred to a physician, stable angina patients can be safely provided with elective dental care. Short morning appointments are preferred. This view has been rebutted, and early morning or late afternoon appointments are advised to be avoided in IHD patients [ ]. Fear, pain, anxiety, and stress can precipitate angina and must be kept to a minimum during the dental visit of an IHD patient. Administration of oral anxiolytics, nitrous oxide or intravenous sedation, and maintaining profound local anesthesia with long-acting anesthetics like bupivacaine minimize the release of endogenous catecholamines. Vasoconstrictors should be used sparingly as their absorption can increase the heart rate. Using 1:100,000 or lesser concentrations of vasoconstrictor and avoiding intravascular injection with proper aspiration are advisable. It is recommended not to use more than one (2 mL) or two cartridges (4 mL) of 2% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine (0.018 to 0.036 mg of adrenaline) for dental procedures in patients with cardiovascular disease [ , ]. If an IHD patient develops chest pain during the dental procedure and angina is suspected, the procedure should be discontinued, and short-acting nitrates along with oxygen should be administered immediately. 0.3–0.6 mg nitroglycerine tablet can be given sublingually and repeated every 5 minutes until the patient is relieved [ ]. Emergency medical assistance must be summoned after three doses (in 15 minutes) if the anginal pain continues. IHD patients are generally on antiplatelets or anticoagulants, and therefore care must be taken in case of excessive bleeding during the dental procedure by local hemostatic techniques. Discontinuation of these medications to perform minor surgical procedures is not recommended [ , ]. If the patient is on anticoagulants, the International Normalized Ratio (INR) should be measured preferably within 24 hours before the procedure. A minor dental surgical procedure can be done safely with INR values in the range of 2.0–4.0 when local measures to control the bleeding are used [ , , , , , , ]. If INR is more than 4.0, no surgical intervention should be performed without the cardiologist’s consultation. 4. Valvular Heart Diseases Valvular heart disease (VHD) is a cardiovascular disease caused due to damage or disease of heart valves. 2.5% of the US population has moderate to severe VHD and its prevalence increases with age [ ]. Various forms of VHD include Degenerative valve disease, Rheumatic heart disease (RHD), and Congenital valve disease [ ]. RHD is a common form of heart disease in developing nations while degenerative valve disease is more common in developed countries [ ]. Common valvular disorders are aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, and mitral regurgitation. 2020 ACC/AHA Guidelines for the management of patients with VHD classified the progression of VHD into 4 stages (Table ) [ ]. Advanced valvular damage causes cardiac dysfunction leading to an increased risk of arrhythmia, infective endocarditis, stroke, and heart failure [ ]. Due to the increased number of VHD patients visiting dental care centers, it has become imperative for dentists to have adequate knowledge of this disease for the safe and effective management of these patients. It is important to identify VHD before performing any dental procedure to avoid the risk of infective endocarditis (IE), risk of excessive bleeding due to anticoagulants, and worsening of the coexisting heart failure [ ]. Dentists can play a vital role in the management of VHD and reducing the risk of complications like IE, stroke, and heart failure which can be fatal for affected patients [ , ]. This can be done through regular dental checkups, patient education, and proper oral hygiene maintenance for these patients which minimize the risk of bacteremia caused by daily activities such as brushing and flossing [ ]. In fact, maintaining good oral hygiene remains the most important element in preventing IE in VHD patients [ ]. 4.1 Prosthetic Valves Most patients with severe VHD need intervention for the valve which includes valve repair or valve replacement (prosthetic valve) of the diseased valve. Prosthetic valves can be mechanical or biological (also called bio-prosthetic valves). Mechanical valves are more durable than bio-prosthetic valves but need lifelong anticoagulants such

through regular dental checkups, patient education, and proper oral hygiene maintenance for these patients which minimize the risk of bacteremia caused by daily activities such as brushing and flossing [ ]. In fact, maintaining good oral hygiene remains the most important element in preventing IE in VHD patients [ ]. 4.1 Prosthetic Valves Most patients with severe VHD need intervention for the valve which includes valve repair or valve replacement (prosthetic valve) of the diseased valve. Prosthetic valves can be mechanical or biological (also called bio-prosthetic valves). Mechanical valves are more durable than bio-prosthetic valves but need lifelong anticoagulants such as warfarin and aspirin. Though all prosthetic valves come along with a risk of thromboembolism, bio-prosthetic valves are less thrombogenic than mechanical valves. The optimum INR range of anticoagulation for mitral mechanical valves is 2.5–3.5 while for aortic valves is 2–3 [ ]. Thrombogenicity of older prosthetic valves is known to be higher and needs INR of up to 4 [ ]. The main clinical implications for patients having prosthetic valves during dental treatment are (a) the need for antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis and (b) perioperative anticoagulation management [ ]. Patients with prosthetic valves need proper dental care with appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent infective endocarditis. Patients with mechanical valves or high-risk patients with bio-prosthetic valves need appropriate anticoagulation with warfarin and aspirin. Anticoagulation in low-risk patients with bio-prosthetic valves can be managed by aspirin alone [ ]. Most dental procedures involve minor bleeding which can be controlled easily and do not require cessation of anticoagulation therapy. They can be performed with an INR of up to 4.0. When anticoagulation cessation is necessary for patients with a high risk of thromboembolism like patients with the mechanical valve but no risk factors, warfarin can be stopped 48–72 hours prior to the procedure (so INR falls below 1.5) and reinitiated within 24 hours of the procedure after control of active bleeding [ , , ]. In mechanical valve patients with the presence of risk factors, warfarin can be stopped 72 hours prior to the procedure and when INR falls below 2.0, heparin can be started which can be stopped 4–6 hours before the procedure [ ]. Anticoagulants are restarted immediately after active bleeding control till therapeutic INR is reached again. Irrespective of the discontinuation of anticoagulation or not, INR must be recorded before any dental procedure involving significant bleeding [ ]. The risk of reducing INR must be weighed against the risk of thromboembolism in consultation with the patient’s physician. Every attempt must be made to control the bleeding even after procedures like extraction or periodontal surgeries using local measures such as suturing, oxidized cellulose, gelatin sponge, thrombin, and tranexamic acid mouthwashes [ ]. 4.2 Infective Endocarditis Infective endocarditis (IE) is an infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, which may involve one or more than one heart valve [ ]. It can affect both native and prosthetic valves. The infection is usually seen in previously damaged heart valves or tissues. This disease has a low incidence but a high overall mortality rate. Thus, primary prevention and proper diagnosis are the main management strategies for this life-threatening disease. In industrialized countries, the estimated annual incidence of IE is 3 to 9 cases per 100,000 individuals [ , , , ]. In-hospital mortality of this disease is 15–22% [ , ] and the 5-year mortality rate is around 40% [ ]. Infective endocarditis is predominantly a bacterial infection with 80% of the cases caused due to streptococci and staphylococci. Formerly, around 60% of native infective endocarditis cases were caused by streptococci. Now staphylococci are more commonly associated with several forms of IE [ , ]. IE is more commonly observed among patients with prosthetic valves, mitral valve prolapse, congenital heart diseases, intracardiac devices, rheumatic heart disease, infective endocarditis history, or a history of cardiac valve surgery [ ]. Prosthetic valve patients with Staphylococcus aureus IE have a high mortality rate of 40% or more [ ]. The healthy valvular endothelium is resistant to microbial colonization but damaged valvular endothelium gets colonized by the circulating bacteria in the bloodstream forming infective vegetation and causing infection. The presence of valvular vegetation is a major criterion in the diagnosis of IE. Severe complications of IE include sepsis, paravalvular extension, embolic events, stroke, and heart failure. Management includes prolonged intravenous antibiotics and valvular surgery [ ]. Various dental therapies and other invasive procedures have been commonly and controversially linked to implanting of bacteria in the heart valves leading to IE. Although IE does not pose an emergency in dental clinics, it is generally associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Management includes prolonged intravenous antibiotics and valvular surgery [ ]. Various dental therapies and other invasive procedures have been commonly and controversially linked to implanting of bacteria in the heart valves leading to IE. Although IE does not pose an emergency in dental clinics, it is generally associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Any dental procedure that aggravates the bleeding and transfers oral bacteria to the bloodstream is an invasive dental procedure, for example scaling, periodontal therapy, exodontia, or any soft tissue surgery. The prevalence of transient bacteremia widely varies for different dental procedures: scaling and root planing (8%–80%), dental extraction (10%–100%), periodontal surgical procedure (36%–88%), and endodontic procedures (up to 20%) [ , , , , , , ]. Even non-invasive dental procedures such as local anesthesia, band placement, and regular practices like tooth brushing and flossing (20–68%), toothpick use (20–40%), and chewing food (7–51%) can cause transient bacteremia [ , , , , , , ]. Thus, the degree of cumulative bacteremia due to routine daily activities is far greater than the infrequent episodes of bacteremia caused by dental procedures. Since 1955, several recommendations have been made by various expert committees and societies for antibiotic prophylaxis in preventing IE secondary to dental procedures [ ]. These guidelines were based on the viewpoint that antibiotic prophylaxis can reduce or eliminate the bacteremia caused by dental or other invasive procedures and prevent IE. However, these recommendations were based on expert opinions and clinical experiences rather than double-blinded randomized controlled clinical trials. No controlled studies have revealed that antibiotic prophylaxis has decreased the incidence of IE. In fact, for many patients, the adverse effects of antibiotic prophylaxis outweigh its benefits. Injudicious antibiotic use can lead to the development of resistant organisms, drug toxicity, and excessive treatment cost [ ]. A Cochrane Database systematic review in 2013 concluded that there is no evidence to ascertain that antibiotic prophylaxis is effective or ineffective in the prevention of IE following dental procedures [ ]. In 2017 an extensive systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted by Cahill TJ et al . [ ] which could not definitely conclude the effectiveness of antibiotic prophylaxis due to limited evidence. The lack of a strong evidence base in favor of antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent IE led to a major revision of AHA guidelines in 2007 wherein the writing committee recommended antibiotic prophylaxis only for the small subcategory of patients who are at the highest risk of developing IE [ ]. UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in 2008 also updated its guidelines and no longer recommended the use of antibiotic prophylaxis in the prevention of IE [ ]. However, in 2016 NICE changed its guidelines which do not recommend antibiotic prophylaxis routinely for patients undergoing dental treatment [ ]. According to this update, antibiotic prophylaxis may be appropriate for selected cases where the dentist perceives the risk of IE to be high or the patient prefers to have the prophylaxis. According to the American Heart Association guidelines 2007, cardiac conditions which have the highest risk of adverse outcome from IE include those with prosthetic cardiac valve or prosthetic material used for cardiac valve repair, history of IE, congenital heart disease (CHD), and cardiac transplant recipients developing cardiac valvulopathy [ , ]. For patients with the aforementioned cardiac conditions, antibiotic prophylaxis is rational for all dental procedures that involve gingival or periapical tissue manipulation or oral mucosal perforation. Prophylaxis is not required for dental procedures such as anesthetic injection through non-infected tissues, dental radiographs, suture removal, biopsies, placement or adjustment of orthodontic or removable prosthodontic appliances, and putting orthodontic brackets [ , ]. Antibiotic prophylaxis is usually given in a single dose 30 to 60 minutes before the dental procedure but can be given up to 2 hours after the procedure. Amoxicillin is the drug of choice for adults (2 grams) and children (50 mg/kg) [ , ]. For adult patients with amoxicillin allergy, azithromycin (500 mg)/clindamycin (600 mg)/clarithromycin (500 mg) or first or second-generation oral cephalosporin like cephalexin (2 grams) can be administered [ , ]. Patients who are unable to take oral medications can be given ampicillin, ceftriaxone, or cefazolin intramuscularly (IM) or intravenously (IV). For patients who are allergic to ampicillin and cannot take oral medications - parenteral ceftriaxone, cefazolin, or clindamycin are recommended [ , ]. The latest American Heart Association scientific statement (2021) recommends that in individuals with allergies to amoxicillin or ampicillin drugs, clindamycin must no longer be used as an oral or parenteral alternative as it may cause more frequent and severe drug reactions [ ]. There is still a dearth of substantial scientific evidence to prove that

For patients who are allergic to ampicillin and cannot take oral medications - parenteral ceftriaxone, cefazolin, or clindamycin are recommended [ , ]. The latest American Heart Association scientific statement (2021) recommends that in individuals with allergies to amoxicillin or ampicillin drugs, clindamycin must no longer be used as an oral or parenteral alternative as it may cause more frequent and severe drug reactions [ ]. There is still a dearth of substantial scientific evidence to prove that dental procedures cause IE in patients with underlying cardiac conditions and antibiotic prophylaxis is worthwhile in preventing IE [ , ]. Even 100% effective antibiotic prophylaxis can prevent only a small number of IE cases. The majority of the IE cases are caused due to bacteremia from routine daily activities including brushing, flossing, and chewing. There must be a fundamental change in the management of patients at high risk of IE by shifting the focus from antibiotic prophylaxis and dental procedures towards access to proper dental care and maintenance of optimal oral health. 5. Anticoagulants Anticoagulant therapy or antithrombotic therapy has been used widely to manage various cardiovascular conditions including myocardial infarction, stroke, and deep vein thrombosis [ ]. The patients on anticoagulant therapy should be handled with proper care and in consultation with the patient’s physician. The patients on anticoagulant medication and undergoing a dental procedure that involves low to medium risk of bleeding can be effectively managed by local hemostatic measures. AHA/ACC/ADA/ESC/SCAI/ACCP guidelines do not suggest the cessation of antiplatelet therapy for procedures involving a low risk of bleeding [ , , ]. The ratio of the patient prothrombin time to the mean prothrombin time raised to the power of international sensitivity index (ISI) value is the INR of the patient. It determines the anticoagulation status of a patient [ ]. It is recommended to check the INR 72 hours prior to an invasive dental procedure in a patient taking long-term anticoagulant therapy and stably anticoagulated on warfarin [ ]. A physiologically normal patient has an INR value of 1, and a therapeutic range of 2.0 to 3.0 is considered safe for most indications due to the reduced risk of thromboembolic events [ ]. In the case of prosthetic heart valves, a higher INR range of 2.5–3.5 is required [ ]. Guidelines on the management of patients on oral anticoagulant therapy (2007) recommend not to discontinue the anticoagulants in patients with stable INR in the range of 2.0–4.0 as the risk of significant bleeding is low for most outpatient dental procedures [ ]. American Academy of Oral Medicine (AAOM) Clinical Practice Statement 2016 stated that an INR value of 3.5 (up to 4.0 by some experts) is safe for moderately invasive dental surgical procedures like simple tooth extractions [ ]. For non-invasive dental procedures, there is no need to maintain this safety margin [ ]. If INR is above 3.5, then the dental procedures should be done with a medical professional consultation weighing the risk of thromboembolism [ ]. In the case of novel non-VKA (non-vitamin K antagonists) and natural/direct anticoagulant therapy (NOAC/DOAC), no discontinuation of the anticoagulant is recommended for low bleeding risk procedures. These procedures can be effectively performed 18–24 hrs after the last dose and anticoagulant can be restarted after 6 hrs of treatment. The medication discontinuation during the medium-risk procedure should be in close communication with the patient’s physician [ , ]. In cases of combined anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy or triple therapy with 2 antiplatelets and one anticoagulant, consult the patient’s physician for individualized management [ ]. The risk of thrombosis on temporary discontinuation of anticoagulants is small but life-threatening. Therapy Warfarin, a vitamin K antagonist, is one of the most common oral anticoagulants used for the prevention and treatment of thromboembolism for more than 50 years. In terms of INR, warfarin has a therapeutic index of 2.0–3.0 [ ]. Factors like narrow therapeutic range along with drug-drug and drug-food interactions limit its use. Over the years, dentists have practiced various perioperative bleeding management strategies for patients on anticoagulant therapy which ranged from continuing the regular dose of anticoagulant to reducing the dose to complete halting or using a bridging anticoagulant like heparin [ ]. Dental procedures are generally categorized as low bleeding risk procedures and studies have concluded that anticoagulation therapy can be safely continued for most of these procedures including dental extractions [ ]. The risk for embolic events after dental surgery appears to vary from 0.02 to 1%. According to a systematic review and meta-analysis (2009) while performing minor dental procedures, continuing the regular warfarin dose does not cause increased bleeding when compared with adjusting or discontinuing its dose [ ]. A 2015 systematic review concluded that for patients undergoing dental extractions, a regular dose of warfarin can be continued if INR is within the therapeutic range [ ]. The benefits of warfarin therapy discontinuation must be weighed carefully against the risk of thromboembolism. If deemed essential, warfarin must be discontinued five days before major surgery and restarted 12–24 hours postoperatively [ ]. INR must be measured a day before surgery to monitor adequate reversal of anticoagulation [ ]. When warfarin therapy is discontinued in patients with an initial INR of 2.0–3.0 for about 4 to 5 days, the INR falls to the normal range (less than 1.5) on the day of surgery which is considered safe for dental procedures and associated with acceptable risk of perioperative bleeding [ ]. The INR reaches the therapeutic range (2.0) after around 3 days of restarting the warfarin therapy [ , , ] (Fig. ). These patients have a subtherapeutic INR for approximately 2–3 days preoperatively and 2 days after surgery during which they are at risk of a thromboembolic event [ , ]. There have been reports of patients experiencing fatal or non-fatal thromboembolic events due to the stoppage of oral anticoagulation for dental treatment [ ]. However, the majority of the patients had no severe effects. According to Todd et al . (2005) [ ], an individualized approach to patients’ systemic conditions by acquiring proper history would be a rational approach in treating patients on warfarin therapy. 5.2 Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACS) The classically used anticoagulant agents are the dicumarinic agents such as Warfarin (Coumadin®) and the acenocoumarol. The disadvantage of these agents is the need of dose adjustment for each patient, their interaction with the consumed foods, and a need to monitor the international normalized ratio (INR) regularly. To overcome these drawbacks, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are being used nowadays [ ]. DOACs are also known as New Oral Anticoagulants (NOACs) and common examples are apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran etexilate, and edoxaban [ ]. The newer agents do not require regular monitoring of anticoagulation and dose adjustment. Studies have also shown no need for NAOC therapy interruption for most dental treatments due to a low incidence of bleeding complications with NAOCs [ , ]. However, the disadvantages of newer agents are higher cost, absence of proper reversal protocols, and lack of post-marketing clinical trials [ ]. The risk of bleeding and adjustment of anticoagulant therapy with newer drugs depend on the type of dental procedure. Low-risk procedures have lesser chances of bleeding and include simple restorations, local anesthetic administration, supragingival scaling, and single-tooth extraction. Moderate risk procedures include extraction of 2 to 4 teeth and gingival surgery of up to 5 teeth. High-risk procedures are associated with a higher risk of bleeding and comprise extracting ≥ 6 teeth, generalized gingival surgery of ≥ 6 teeth, and multiple dental implant placement [ ]. According to the available evidence, DOAC therapy can be continued safely for low-to-medium risk dental procedures as the involved risk of bleeding is low. In case bleeding occurs, local hemostatic measures can be used to manage it [ ]. It is recommended not to perform these dental procedures during the peak concentrations of DOAC therapy but close to the end of the dosing cycle. Another alternative is to administer the DOAC after the procedure instead of before or perform the procedure 12–24 hours after the DOAC administration. In case of invasive or surgical dental procedure involving moderate to high risk of bleeding, it is recommended by manufacturers to discontinue edoxaban and rivaroxaban 24 hours prior and apixaban 48 hours before the procedure [ , , ]. If discontinuation of DOAC is necessary, it should be reinitiated on the same day of the dental procedure. Overall, there

dental procedures during the peak concentrations of DOAC therapy but close to the end of the dosing cycle. Another alternative is to administer the DOAC after the procedure instead of before or perform the procedure 12–24 hours after the DOAC administration. In case of invasive or surgical dental procedure involving moderate to high risk of bleeding, it is recommended by manufacturers to discontinue edoxaban and rivaroxaban 24 hours prior and apixaban 48 hours before the procedure [ , , ]. If discontinuation of DOAC is necessary, it should be reinitiated on the same day of the dental procedure. Overall, there is limited evidence at hand on the dental management of patients taking NAOCs and further studies are strongly recommended. 5.3 Bleeding Complications The commonly used anticoagulants or the antiplatelets are the clopidogrel (Plavix®), ticlopidine (Ticlid®), prasugrel (Effient®), ticagrelor (Brilinta®), and/or asprin.The antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy during the dental treatment increases the risk of bleeding which can be significant but generally not serious. Anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs need not be stopped for procedures that induce minor bleeding, such as bridge placement, three teeth removal, and scaling procedures [ , ]. If multiple extractions are planned, it has to be performed three teeth at a time in multiple visits choosing the most affected at the first visit [ , ]. Most cases of perioperative or postoperative bleeding can be managed by minimizing the surgical trauma, limiting the area of surgery, primary closure of the surgical wound with sutures, applying pressure with gauze for 15–30 minutes, or using local hemostats such as tranexamic acid-soaked bite swabs, gelatin sponge, EACA (Epsilon amino caproic acid), 4.8% tranexamic acid mouthwash (4 times a day for 2 minutes, 1–2 days postsurgery), calcium sulfate (CaS), fibrin sponge, autologous fibrin glue, resorbable oxycellulose dressing and N-butyl-2-cyanoacrylate glue (NBCA) [ , , , ]. The incidence of bleeding that local hemostatic methods could not manage ranges from 0 to 3.5% [ , ]. Postoperative measures for the patients on oral anticoagulants to prevent bleeding include adequate resting, no vigorous rinsing or sucking; avoiding hot or hard foodstuffs that can disturb the socket with the tongue or any foreign object [ ]. NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors should not be prescribed for analgesia to patients taking antithrombotic medications [ ]. 6. Arrhythmias Cardiac arrhythmia or dysrhythmia can be described as a disturbance in the generation or conduction of cardiac electrical impulses which causes improper heart functioning [ ]. Common heart rhythm abnormalities include premature atrial or ventricular beats, sinus bradycardia, and sinus tachycardia [ , ]. The most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia found clinically is atrial fibrillation (AF) with approximately 46.3 million patients suffering from it globally [ ]. Its incidence increases with obesity [ ] and age, with 9% of the patients above 80 years having AF [ ]. Dysrhythmia can be present in healthy people, patients on certain medications, with cardiovascular problems, or other systemic diseases. Many individuals with arrhythmia are asymptomatic, and the abnormality is generally found during a routine examination. However, others can present a variety of symptoms like dizziness, shortness of breath, weakness, syncope, and chest pain (angina). Elderly patients with compromised cardiac conditions can even develop myocardial ischemia, shock, or congestive heart failure due to arrhythmia [ , , , ]. Patients with certain cardiac arrhythmias like atrial fibrillation have more chances of having ischemic events during stressful dental treatment or when excessive local anesthesia with a vasoconstrictor is administered. In addition, the association of arrhythmias with various systemic diseases and their potentially life-threatening nature make it imperative for dentists to identify and adopt appropriate measures to manage this cardiac problem promptly and effectively. Arrhythmias are generally managed by antiarrhythmic drugs, cardiac pacemakers, cardioversion, or surgical intervention. Beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers are the most frequently prescribed medications. However, these drugs are associated with oral side effects like xerostomia and gingival overgrowth. These patients may seek attention from the dentist due to abnormal gingiva appearance (gingival enlargement), bleeding, pain in the gums, or dryness of mouth, and must be treated with caution. Cardiac pacemakers and automatic implantable cardioverter defibrillators (AICD) detect abnormal heart rhythm and help to restore the normal rhythm [ ]. Cardioversion is the restoration of the sinus rhythm of the heart using medications or electric shock [ ]. Identification of the patients with arrhythmia or those susceptible to developing arrhythmia, obtaining a detailed medical history, assessing vital signs, and consultation with the patient’s physician are vital steps to prevent the development of any severe complication during or after dental treatment. High-risk patients must be referred to a well-equipped hospital facility. In a dental office, stress and anxiety must be minimized to prevent the precipitation of arrhythmia. This can be achieved by premedication like short-acting benzodiazepines the night before or one hour before the

restoration of the sinus rhythm of the heart using medications or electric shock [ ]. Identification of the patients with arrhythmia or those susceptible to developing arrhythmia, obtaining a detailed medical history, assessing vital signs, and consultation with the patient’s physician are vital steps to prevent the development of any severe complication during or after dental treatment. High-risk patients must be referred to a well-equipped hospital facility. In a dental office, stress and anxiety must be minimized to prevent the precipitation of arrhythmia. This can be achieved by premedication like short-acting benzodiazepines the night before or one hour before the appointment or by using nitrous oxide-oxygen inhalation. Short morning dental appointments with a simple treatment plan are preferred. Local anesthetics with vasoconstrictors must be used judiciously as excessive epinephrine can precipitate arrhythmia or other unwanted cardiovascular complications [ , , ]. The amount of vasoconstrictor should not exceed 0.04–0.054 mg per appointment [ ]. In addition, vasoconstrictors like epinephrine are contraindicated in patients with refractory arrhythmias and must be used carefully in patients having implanted defibrillators or pacemakers [ ]. There has been conflicting evidence in the literature regarding potential electromagnetic interference by electronic dental instruments like ultrasonic scalers, apex locators, and electrosurgical units in the functioning of cardiovascular implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) like pacemakers or implantable defibrillators. Many earlier in-vitro studies have found that dental electronic devices interfere with the functioning of CIEDs. Miller et al . [ ] reported significant electromagnetic interference by electrosurgery units, ultrasonic bath cleaners, and ultrasonic scaling devices with pacemakers in a dental setup. Older pacemakers were unipolar and unshielded or poorly shielded. The newer ones are bipolar with better shielding which lowers the risk of malfunction due to electromagnetic interference [ ]. Electric pulp testers, dental handpieces, amalgamators, curing lights, and sonic scalers have been reported to be safer [ ]. Also, piezoelectric scalers are safer to use than magnetostrictive devices in patients with CIEDs [ , , ]. Antibiotic coverage is not advocated by American Heart Association (AHA) for patients using devices like pacemakers and automatic defibrillators during invasive dental treatment [ ]. Studies mention that an increased likelihood of electromagnetic interferences is seen if the device comes within 37.5 cm of the CIED or lead wire [ ]. Arrhythmia patients may receive anticoagulant therapy, and therefore it becomes crucial for the dentist to determine the level of anticoagulation prior to any invasive procedure. Most dental procedures (including minor oral surgical procedures) can be performed if the International Normalized Ratio (INR) is 3.5 or less on the day of the procedure [ ]. If the patient develops arrhythmia during dental treatment, the procedure should be deferred, and the patient must be urgently referred for medical evaluation. Oxygen should be provided, and the patient’s vital signs like body temperature, pulse, respiratory frequency, and blood pressure should be assessed. Loss of consciousness or collapse may indicate life-threatening arrhythmia or cardiac arrest, and emergency medical services must be activated immediately. Performing vagal maneuvers and placing the patient in Trendelenburg’s position can be helpful [ ]. If no pulse is detected, cardiopulmonary resuscitation must be initiated using an automated external defibrillator without any delay. 7. Use of Local Anaesthetics with Vasoconstrictor Dental treatment is often associated with pain, fear, and anxiety. Stress and anxiety may lead to exaggerated endogenous catecholamine release from the adrenal medulla, causing hemodynamic disturbances [ , ]. In patients with underlying cardiovascular pathologies like hypertensive heart disease, ischemic heart disease, arrhythmias, or heart transplantation patients, inadequate local anesthesia may cause massive endogenous adrenaline release provoking cardiovascular complications. So, pain control and stress reduction are essential for patients undergoing dental treatment, particularly those with underlying cardiac disease. Local anesthetics with vasoconstrictors (like epinephrine) in dentistry impart prolonged anesthesia, reduced systemic toxicity, and optimal bleeding control [ , ]. Though the use of epinephrine in local anesthetics is common for healthy patients, its use is still debatable for cardiac patients due to its potential risk of causing unwanted cardiovascular effects. However, many authors have reported no clinically significant hemodynamic changes during dental treatment in healthy people or patients with mild to moderate coronary disease [ , , , , , ]. The dose of vasoconstrictor used in dental treatment is significantly less than the dose used during the treatment of anaphylaxis for cardiac arrest. For example, one cartridge of local anesthetic of 1.8 mL in volume with 1:100,000 epinephrine contains only 0.018 mg of vasoconstrictor [ ]. This small amount of vasoconstrictor used in dentistry poses little risk than the more significant risk from the massive endogenous epinephrine release due to improper control of pain and anxiety during dental treatment in cardiac patients. Thus, if administered carefully with aspiration, the concentration and amount of vasoconstrictor used in dentistry are generally not contraindicated for cardiac

vasoconstrictor used in dental treatment is significantly less than the dose used during the treatment of anaphylaxis for cardiac arrest. For example, one cartridge of local anesthetic of 1.8 mL in volume with 1:100,000 epinephrine contains only 0.018 mg of vasoconstrictor [ ]. This small amount of vasoconstrictor used in dentistry poses little risk than the more significant risk from the massive endogenous epinephrine release due to improper control of pain and anxiety during dental treatment in cardiac patients. Thus, if administered carefully with aspiration, the concentration and amount of vasoconstrictor used in dentistry are generally not contraindicated for cardiac patients. However, it is better to use the lowest possible dose of vasoconstrictor to achieve adequate local anesthesia while treating patients with “stable” cardiac problems. Therefore, up to 0.04 mg or 40 μ g of epinephrine, i.e., one or two carpules of 1.8 mL anesthetic solution with epinephrine 1:100,000 concentration is safe for controlled hypertensives and/or coronary disease patients [ , ]. Heart conditions that contraindicate the use of vasoconstrictors in dentistry include [ ]: (a) Unstable angina (b) Recent myocardial infarction (c) Recent coronary artery bypass surgery (d) Refractory arrhythmias (e) Untreated or uncontrolled severe hypertension (f) Untreated or uncontrolled congestive heart failure Also, it is contraindicated to use epinephrine impregnated retraction cords, intraligamentary, and intrabony injections in these patients due to adverse hydrodynamic effects similar to I.V. epinephrine injection [ ]. Though local anesthetics can lead to a decrease in the rate of amide metabolism in hypertensive patients taking beta-blockers [ ], generally non-epinephrine-containing local anesthetics do not have significant drug interactions [ ]. Drug interactions mostly stem from the incorporated vasoconstrictor [ ]. For example, epinephrine can interact with commonly used antihypertensives like non-selective beta-blockers causing significant hypertensive episodes [ ] and reflex bradycardia [ ]. Though the response is dose-dependent and rarely seen in dental clinics, the dentist must be careful in using vasoconstrictors in patients with significant cardiac disease due to the serious sequelae of this drug combination. Agents like clonidine [ ] and dexmedetomidine [ ] can be used as safer alternatives to epinephrine with the local anesthetic solution in hypertensive patients. In such patients, it can also be prudent to use lidocaine, prilocaine, and mepivacaine solutions without vasoconstrictor [ ]. 8. Conclusions Dental treatment, although considered safe, can be life-threatening if medical problems of the patient, especially cardiac disorders are ignored. A thorough medical and drug history from each patient at every appointment and extensive knowledge of the risk factors and clinical manifestations of various cardiac diseases can prevent many medical adversities in the dental clinic. A comprehensive treatment plan formulated in collaboration with the patient’s cardiologist can help avoid potential hazards during dental treatment for a cardiac patient. All drug prescriptions, surgical interventions, and overall management strategies should conform to the latest guidelines and protocols available. Dentists should also identify and judiciously manage any medical emergency that can occur while the patient is on the dental chair. Stress before and during dental treatment is normal for any patient, but it can cause medical complications in cardiac patients. So pharmacologic agents can be prescribed to induce relaxation and reduce stress in these patients. Also, morning appointments should be preferred as mornings are more relaxing, and in case of any unforeseen situation, there is sufficient time to manage it. Comprehensive knowledge of the dentist about cardiac conditions with multidisciplinary planning supported by an evidence-based approach is indispensable in imparting quality and safe dental care to this vulnerable cohort of dental patients.

chunks.content: Background Heart failure (HF) in pediatrics can be secondary to a variety of causes, including structural abnormalities from congenital heart disease (CHD), myocardial abnormalities such as genetic cardiomyopathies, and acquired causes such as anthracycline-induced cardiomyopathies. The annual incidence of HF is reported to be between 0.9 and 3 per 100,000 children in Europe and results from a combination of increased preload, increased afterload, decreased myocardial contractility, and/or arrhythmias leading to a mismatch between cardiac output and the body’s metabolic demands. HF is common in patients diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathies, with data from an Australian registry study demonstrating that 89.7% of cases will present in HF. Meanwhile, for children with CHD, HF symptomatology has been reported to occur between 6.2% and 23.7% of patients. , The importance of nutrition in critical illness, such as HF, in the pediatric population has been well described, with studies suggesting that malnutrition is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. The cause of malnutrition in pediatric patients with HF is the result of increased energy expenditure and decreased energy supply, secondary to a complex interplay of factors such as decreased intake, malabsorption, and existing in a catabolic state. , The problems associated with malnutrition are further compounded by deficiencies of certain micronutrients that can exacerbate HF symptomatology. The details of the pathophysiology of malnutrition and HF have been well described in Lewis et al’s 2018 paper. The aim of this review article is to describe approaches to assessing the nutritional status in pediatric patients with HF and how nutrition can be used to optimize the clinical state of children with HF. How to assess nutritional status and requirements Malnutrition remains a major concern in children with HF and is associated with poor clinical outcomes, including delayed postoperative recovery, higher infection rates, and increased morbidity and mortality. , Causes of malnutrition arise from the unique metabolic challenges faced by these patients, including metabolic changes, reduced dietary intake, and disruptions in nutrient absorption. , Chronic conditions such as CHD and cardiomyopathy, both of which can lead to HF, frequently lead to growth delays and protein-energy malnutrition, with nearly half of these patients demonstrating anthropometric indicators of malnutrition during their treatment journey. , Accurately assessing nutritional status in children with HF is challenging because standard markers, such as weight, weight for age, and BMI (Body Mass Index) z-scores, are often impaired by confounding factors such as fluid retention. These issues reduce the reliability of traditional methods, leaving practitioners to explore alternative strategies for assessing nutritional status in this population. Recently, there has been a move toward using validated assessment tools such as the Subjective Global Nutritional Assessment (SGNA). The SGNA has been validated in the pediatric population and it has a significant role in identifying malnutrition in children with CHD due to its comprehensive nature that evaluates multiple dimensions of nutritional health. It includes a detailed assessment of medical history, feeding practices, gastrointestinal functionality, and physical measurements such as weight, height, mid-arm circumference, and skin folds along with the respective z-scores. , , It emphasizes trends rather than single measurements, which allows the SGNA to identify malnutrition in children who may be missed when anthropometrics alone are not accurate when edema is present. In adult literature, body composition (specifically decreased muscle mass) is reported as being associated with increased morbidity and mortality in patients with HF, with both dual-energy X-ray absorption and BOD-POD scans are gaining traction as noninvasive ways of objective quantification. , While there is currently no literature reporting the use of either of these technologies in the pediatric HF population, the possibility is intriguing. However, there are some limitations that come with the use of dual-energy X-ray absorption scans for nutritional assessments in children, given the radiation exposure and limited availability in clinical settings. For this to be justified, there would need to be further validation of BOD-POD in a research setting, as currently, the limited information available suggests significant technical challenges. Children with HF have variable energy requirements, with some having increased demands (hypermetabolism) due to chronic tachycardia, increased myocardial workload, systemic inflammation, and neurohormonal activation, while others may have lower energy needs (hypometabolism) due to reduced physical activity and worsening organ function. This variation makes it difficult to use predictive equations alone to determine energy requirements and for prevention or treatment of malnutrition. Therefore, other tools such as indirect calorimetry are important when traditional equations are less reliable. Indirect calorimetry is considered the gold standard for determining basal metabolic rate (BMR) and is patient-specific, with direct measures of resting energy expenditure through measurements of oxygen consumption (VO 2 ) and carbon dioxide production (VCO 2 ). makes it difficult to use predictive equations alone to determine energy requirements and for prevention or treatment of malnutrition. Therefore, other tools such as indirect calorimetry are important when traditional equations are less reliable. Indirect calorimetry is considered the gold standard for determining basal metabolic rate (BMR) and is patient-specific, with direct measures of resting energy expenditure through measurements of oxygen consumption (VO 2 ) and carbon dioxide production (VCO 2 ). This tool can be advantageous in determining the caloric needs of pediatric patients with HF, as the metabolic state varies significantly based on disease severity. BMR represents the energy your body requires to perform essential functions at rest, such as maintaining your heartbeat, respiratory processes, brain activity, and cellular repair. It accounts for the largest part of total energy expenditure, which makes it a critical factor when estimating overall energy requirements. Various studies have shown that the use of predictive equations inaccurately estimated the energy expenditure and, therefore, the energy needs of these patients. , , Importantly, Lewis et al highlighted that energy requirements can be as much as 2 times higher in children with HF than what predictive equations suggest, underscoring the hypermetabolic state observed in many of these patients. However, these energy needs are dynamic and can significantly shift postoperatively or during other stages of treatment. For example, after surgeries such as the Fontan procedure, indirect calorimetry has revealed the variability in resting energy expenditure ranging from hypermetabolic to hypometabolic states depending on factors such as age, recovery progress, and inflammation. Due to this variability, indirect calorimetry will not only ensure accurate initial assessments but should be conducted serially to adjust energy delivery as the child's condition changes. Access to indirect calorimetry for determining energy requirements in pediatric patients with HF can be challenging; hence, clinicians may rely on the validated predictive equations and tailored clinical judgment. We know that formulas such as the Schofield or WHO (World Health Organization) equations, which estimate BMR based on age, weight, height, and sex, are widely used but can yield variability, potentially underestimating or overestimating energy needs. Close and serial monitoring of patient-specific growth patterns, weight trends, and clinical indicators remains essential to accurately address energy needs, promote growth and recovery, and prevent risks associated with underfeeding or overfeeding. A study conducted by Marino et al has shown that nutritional care must be a central component in the management of patients with CHD. They used a protocol that involved early identification of growth failure by regular and serial anthropometric checks, individualizing energy needs, optimizing feeding methods, pre and post op nutrition support, and ongoing monitoring and adjustments. This data support that using an assessment tool, such as the SGNA, serially can be helpful to monitor a patient's progress of malnutrition and growth. How do we deliver adequate nutrition? The choice of nutrition and route of providing nutrition in children with HF can play an important role in ensuring they are meeting their metabolic demands and nutritional requirements. Children with HF can struggle to absorb nutrients due to a combination of increased gut wall edema and decreased gut perfusion, with adult literature suggesting that patients with HF have a 30% to 45% decrease in blood flow through the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and celiac artery compared to healthy patients. With this in mind, it is important to select feeds that can be easily digested and absorbed. The use of elemental feeds, which consist of amino acids and predigested proteins, can help mitigate the absorption challenges and feeding intolerance which is often encountered. An additional challenge faced with providing enteral nutrition is that patients are often fluid-restricted as part of their HF management. In context of this, feeds may need to be fortified to meet protein and energy requirements. Recently, blended food diets have started to replace formula-based diets, due to the evidence that they can help with some of the gastrointestinal symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea which can be seen with commercial formulas, as well caregiver preference view this diet as more “natural,” and blended diets improve the sense of normalcy with feeds. , Current recommendations from the British Dietetic Association with respect to blended diets include: a. Decisions to use blended diets should be made by a multidisciplinary team. From our institutional experience, this team should include the parents, dietician, cardiologist, HF nurse, occupational therapist, speech and language therapist, and the child depending on their age and maturity. b. Adequate food hygiene standards must be able to be maintained during diet preparation. c. Patients should be able to tolerate bolus feeds (given the risk of bacterial growth in food kept at room temperature). d. The diet should be able to meet the nutritional requirements of the child. Decisions to use blended diets should be made by a multidisciplinary team. From our institutional experience, this team should include the parents, dietician, cardiologist, HF nurse, occupational therapist, speech and language therapist, and the child depending on their age and maturity. b. Adequate food hygiene standards must be able to be maintained during diet preparation. c. Patients should be able to tolerate bolus feeds (given the risk of bacterial growth in food kept at room temperature). d. The diet should be able to meet the nutritional requirements of the child. In patients with HF symptomatology, it is particularly important to ensure that these feeds do not exceed the daily recommended sodium intake, as high sodium diets can result in fluid retention and clinical symptoms of fluid overload. Specific contraindications to a blended diet include children unable to tolerate gastric feeds (requiring transpyloric feeding), children at increased risk of foodborne infections, children who require a nasogastric tube (NGT) rather than a gastrostomy tube, and infants under 6 months of age. A further factor to consider is the route by which the nutrition is provided. The factors to consider are whether a child can take adequate nutrition on their own orally or whether a child requires a feeding tube. The choice of feeding tube is predominantly driven by feeding tolerance and risk of a procedure. For children who can be fed into their stomach, an NGT can be utilized as can a gastrostomy (G-tube). Both G-tube and NGT feeding have been demonstrated as an effective way to provide nutrition for children who are not able to meet their goals orally. , G-tubes are typically thought to be more secure than NGTs; however, the insertion is more invasive, with a risk associated with the need for general anesthesia in a patient with HF and the ongoing risk of stoma site infections. , Despite the perceived benefit of G-tubes having more stability than NGTs, a 2017 study by Khalil et al comparing infants on home NGT feeds with those on home G-tube feeds found that infants with G-tubes had more emergency department presentations for device-related issues in the first 6 months postdischarge than those with NGTs, and that 39.1% of those presentations were due to G-tube dislodgement. This would suggest that for patients for whom a G-tube would pose an unnecessary anesthetic risk that the use of an NGT is a reasonable alternative. A final option for enteral feeding is the use of transpyloric feeds. Transpyloric feeds can be beneficial in that the nutrition is delivered directly to the site of absorption and can help bypass difficulties with gastric emptying, vomiting, and aspiration. , However, the downside to transpyloric feeds is that these feeds need to be given continuously rather than as bolus feeds. This not only provides social limitations in that children will be attached to feeds for most of the day, but also limits feed options such as no longer being able to have blended diets. There is a subgroup of pediatric patients with HF who are either unable to absorb or unable to tolerate adequate amounts of enteral feeds, who will require parenteral nutrition. While there are no specific guidelines for pediatric patients with HF, the American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition guidelines exist for the use of parenteral nutrition in critically unwell patients. Importantly, the inability to tolerate enteral nutrition is suggestive of advanced HF, and treating teams should be considering referring to an advanced HF service for consideration of ventricular assist device (VAD) support. , How can we optimize heart function through nutrition? The importance of adequate macronutrients has been well described in patients with HF, with a recent focus on supplementation of micronutrients as part of the goal of optimizing nutrition in patients with HF. Below, we discuss key macro and micronutrients that should be considered when trying to optimize. Macronutrients Protein Decreased protein intake in both adults and children with HF has been associated with loss of skeletal muscle loss and increased mortality. , Children with chronic diseases such as HF can develop protein-energy wasting, otherwise known as cachexia, secondary to increased BMR, lean muscle wasting, and inefficient use of fat for energy. In context of this, there have been suggestions that infants should have a caloric intake of 150 kcal/kg/d and children and adolescents 25 to 30 kcal/kg/day with 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day of this being protein, or an increase in protein by 50% to 100% of the dietary reference intake. Adequate protein intake is essential to ensure there is a consistent supply of amino acids which is essential for protein synthesis, tissue repair, and energy. , Furthermore, certain amino acids such as carnitine or glutathione (made from glycine, cysteine, and glutamic acid) are thought to be associated with cellular function of the heart. Carbohydrates

Adequate protein intake is essential to ensure there is a consistent supply of amino acids which is essential for protein synthesis, tissue repair, and energy. , Furthermore, certain amino acids such as carnitine or glutathione (made from glycine, cysteine, and glutamic acid) are thought to be associated with cellular function of the heart. Carbohydrates Adequate carbohydrate intake is important as it is the primary source of energy for the brain. The current recommendation in pediatric HF is to keep daily carbohydrate intake to 6 g/kg/day. In a normal heart, 60% to 90% of cardiac adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is provided by fatty acid oxidization; however, in patients with HF, there is thought to be a switch to glucose oxidation, as carbohydrates are more oxygen-efficient than fatty acids. This would suggest ensuring adequate carbohydrate intake is an important part of optimizing nutrition for patients in HF. A recent pilot study in the adult diabetic cardiomyopathy population suggested that while a low-carbohydrate diet improved weight loss and quality of life, there was no improvement in their Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire summary score, and acknowledged further studies are needed to assess the effects of a low-carbohydrate diet on cardiac function. A potential explanation for the benefit of low low-carbohydrate diet is that it mimics the effects of sodium glucose cotranspoort-2 inhibitors, which have been demonstrated to be effective in HF management. However, this study has only been performed in a specific subtype of cardiomyopathy and may not be generalizable to pediatric patients with HF. At this stage, there is no convincing evidence to recommend low-carbohydrate diets in the pediatric population. Fatty acids Omega-3 fatty acids supplementation in the adult HF population has been demonstrated to be associated with improved cardiac function, decreased risk of arrhythmias, and reduced hospitalizations. This is likely in part due to the fact that omega-3 is associated with lowering inflammation and helping with ventricular remodeling. Omega-3 has been demonstrated to have additional benefits in the pediatric population, including supporting vision and cognitive function. , In light of these benefits, we would suggest supplementation if children are not reaching the adequate intakes outlined by the National Institutes of Health. Micronutrients Iron Iron deficiency is common in patients with HF symptoms, secondary to abnormalities in iron storage, reduced intake, and decreased availability of iron through the reticuloendothelial system. , As cardiomyocytes have high metabolic demand, the presence of iron deficiency and the resulting impairment of mitochondrial ATP generation worsen cardiac dysfunction and HF symptomatology. , Studies into iron deficiency in the pediatric HF population have demonstrated that iron deficiency is associated with worse ventricular function. , While both these studies demonstrated a decrease in function associated with iron deficiency, they had conflicting results with regards to longer-term sequelae such as need for a VAD, death, or transplant, , which needs to be taken in context of the fact that iron deficiency was not routinely monitored. Use of iron supplementation has been well studied in the adult population, which suggested that oral iron supplementation has limited impacts on a patients’ clinical status, while intravenous supplementation is associated with reduced hospitalizations, improved functional status, and quality of life. In context of this current adult guidelines from the European Society of Cardiology and the American Heart Association recommend using ferric carboxymaltose, an intravenous formulation to treat iron deficiency, with 1 study suggesting that there can be benefit even in the absence of anemia. , , A recent study in the pediatric population examining the use of oral iron supplementations demonstrated similar results to the adult IRONOUT-HF study, which was that oral supplementation was ineffective at increasing serum iron levels. The explanation for this is likely a combination of reduced absorption due to gut wall edema, and the fact that as HF is a chronic inflammatory state, there may be an increase in hepcidin inhibiting iron absorption. In context of the fact that iron deficiency has been demonstrated to be associated with worse function, and may potentially increase the risk of adverse sequelae, we would recommend routine monitoring and supplementation, While standard iron deficiency guidelines suggest oral supplementation initially before escalating to intravenous, given oral iron has been demonstrated at being ineffective at raising serum iron levels in patients with HF, consideration should be given to intravenous iron as first line therapy in all patients, irrespective of whether they are hospitalized or at home. Selenium Selenium is a micronutrient that is incorporated into selenoproteins, which mediate the cardiovascular system via inflammatory and antioxidative effects. Deficiencies in selenium have been associated

associated with worse function, and may potentially increase the risk of adverse sequelae, we would recommend routine monitoring and supplementation, While standard iron deficiency guidelines suggest oral supplementation initially before escalating to intravenous, given oral iron has been demonstrated at being ineffective at raising serum iron levels in patients with HF, consideration should be given to intravenous iron as first line therapy in all patients, irrespective of whether they are hospitalized or at home. Selenium Selenium is a micronutrient that is incorporated into selenoproteins, which mediate the cardiovascular system via inflammatory and antioxidative effects. Deficiencies in selenium have been associated with a specific form of cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease). , However, even in the absence of Keshan disease, studies have demonstrated that patients with dilated cardiomyopathy tend to have lower serum levels of selenium compared to those without it. , While there have been no studies determining the effectiveness of routine selenium supplementation in pediatric patients with HF, an analysis of patients from the BIOSTAT-CHF study, suggested in older adults that selenium supplementation may improve patient outcomes, however this was an observational study, and there were multiple confounding factors including the coadministration of coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10), and as such they recommended further prospective clinical trials to determine the benefits of selenium supplementation. Zinc Zinc plays an important role in cell membrane stabilization by acting as a cofactor for enzymes involved in the antioxidant systems and by inhibiting pro-oxidant enzymes. Deficiencies in zinc have been demonstrated to be associated with dilated cardiomyopathies, coronary artery injury, and myocardial infarction and reduced function. Dietary deficiencies may be compounded in patients with HF due to activation of atrial natriuretic peptide and subsequent increased urinary excretion of zinc. There is some early evidence to suggest that zinc supplementation may be beneficial if deficient, but this is controversial as current American Heart Association guidelines suggest that there is no direct benefit from routine supplementation. Vitamin D Patients with HF are at risk of vitamin D deficiency due to a combination of renal insufficiency, medications, and poor nutrition. Vitamin D plays an essential role not only in bone health, but also with regards to supporting myocardial contractility and cardiac remodeling. , There is observational evidence that vitamin D deficiency is associated with worse outcomes for patients with HF, and small studies in the adult population demonstrating an improvement in ejection fraction with vitamin D supplementation. , While 25(OH[Hydroxy]) vitamin D levels of ≥20 ng/ml (≥50 nmol/liter) are typically considered sufficient, there has been suggestions that in patients with HF, having a 25(OH) vitamin D level <30 ng/ml (<75 nmol/liter) may actually be insufficient. While there currently is no specific recommendations for what the target 25(OH) vitamin D level should be in pediatric patients with HF, given the fact that they may require higher than standard targets to be considered sufficient, it would be reasonable to continue to follow the suggestion of Lewis et al, and aim to keep serum 25(OH) vitamin D levels 32 ng/ml (≥80 nmol/liter), to ensure an adequate buffer. There are currently no guidelines as to how frequently therapy should be monitored in patients with HF. We would suggest using a similar approach to that which is recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics for monitoring vitamin D levels in rickets patients, whereby this is assessed at diagnosis, then if treatment is commenced, 3 months after this to ensure an adequate response, and then annually. Coenzyme Q10 CoQ10 is involved in the synthesis of ATP, cell membrane stabilization, and has antioxidant properties which may help prevent cardiac myocyte injury. Dietary deficiency in CoQ10 is reported to be associated with lower ejection fraction, increased NT-proBNP levels, and worse New York Heart Association functional class. A recent Cochrane review suggests that CoQ10 may reduce all-cause cardiovascular mortality, but that the current evidence is not robust enough to draw conclusive recommendations with regards to the benefit of CoQ10 supplementation and HF optimization. What is the family perspective on nutrition? Qualitative analyses have shown that a diagnosis of HF is a source of significant stress for parents and caregivers. , One of the identified stressors that has been reported is feeding and nutrition. The reason that feeding and nutrition is a stressor is multifactorial, resulting from a combination of feeding and weight gain being considered a surrogate marker for disease progression, and that nutrition is typically a basic need provided by caregivers. , In children with complex health needs, who are highly medicalized with very little normalcy, striving to orally feed can result from a parent hoping that their child can participate in something that is considered “normal.” A desire for children to feed orally has led to the rise of rapid tube weaning programs, which aim to use a multidisciplinary approach to rapidly transition a child from NGT

is a stressor is multifactorial, resulting from a combination of feeding and weight gain being considered a surrogate marker for disease progression, and that nutrition is typically a basic need provided by caregivers. , In children with complex health needs, who are highly medicalized with very little normalcy, striving to orally feed can result from a parent hoping that their child can participate in something that is considered “normal.” A desire for children to feed orally has led to the rise of rapid tube weaning programs, which aim to use a multidisciplinary approach to rapidly transition a child from NGT or G-tube to full oral feeding over a period of weeks. , While these programs have been demonstrated to be successful and show that at 1 year post wean children are gaining weight appropriately, they are associated with a decrease in both protein and energy intake at the time of wean, with associated weight loss. , There have been no studies specifically examining rapid tube weans in the HF population. Considering the importance of adequate caloric and protein intake in our cohort, we would recommend proceeding with caution in this group, as they may not tolerate the period of decreased energy intake and weight loss as well as children without underlying HF. Conclusion Managing nutrition in children with HF is a vital part of their medical care. These children often have higher than expected metabolic demands, and assessing these can be challenging. Ensuring children are taking the right types of nutrition, via the most appropriate route is paramount to ensuring they are meeting their nutritional goals, acknowledging that if they are not able to reach this with enteral nutrition alone, this would be an indication to consider advanced HF therapies such as VAD support. Adequate protein intake is essential for children with HF, and feeding regimes and diets should be designed to target a daily goal of 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day. While there has been some considerations of low-carbohydrate diets in specific adult HF populations, at this stage, we would recommend continuing with standard carbohydrate intake. From a supplementation perspective, there is currently evidence to suggest supplementation with omega-3, vitamin D, and intravenous iron to improve nutritional outcomes. While there is currently no conclusive evidence to support routine supplementation of micronutrients such as zinc, selenium, or CoQ10, this is an area of evolving interest. As feeding and nutrition play such an integral role in the management of children with HF, it is important to consider the impact this can have on families, and to work as a team with the families to ensure that the child’s clinical state and the mental health of the family are both being supported during this journey. chunks.content: Central Message Prehabilitation in cardiac surgery warrants a standardized, personalized, and evidence-based approach to improve outcomes and enable broader, consistent implementation within ERAS pathways. Perspective Prehabilitation offers a valuable opportunity to improve cardiac surgery outcomes but is limited by variable evidence and lack of standardization. A multidimensional, adaptable approach, which includes physical, psychological, nutritional, and sociodemographic factors, may establish prehabilitation as core to equitable, patient-centered cardiac care. The concept of prehabilitation, which involves enhancing a patient's functional capacity before they undergo surgery to improve baseline health, thereby increasing resilience to the surgical procedure, , , has gained attention across multiple surgical disciplines. Rooted in the idea that patients undergoing major operations are not merely passive recipients of care but active participants, prehabilitation commonly encompasses 1 or more of the following elements undertaken before surgery: physical training, nutritional optimization, psychological support, and risk factor modification. This proactive approach aims to prepare patients for the physiological stress of surgery, with the ultimate goal of enhancing recovery and reducing complications. Although originally developed in the context of oncologic and orthopedic surgery, , prehabilitation is now being explored in thoracic and cardiovascular contexts. , , Institutional review board approval and consent were not required for this article. In cardiac surgery, prehabilitation programs typically focus on improving cardiorespiratory fitness and functional status through interventions such as aerobic exercise, resistance training, and inspiratory muscle training (IMT). These modalities have been shown to improve preoperative performance on validated assessments and patient-reported quality-of-life (QoL) metrics. , , , Several studies have demonstrated that these programs are not only safe in the preoperative cardiac population but may also improve clinical outcomes by reducing postoperative complications, shortening hospital stays, and improving early recovery trajectories. , Beyond exercise, emerging evidence suggests that incorporating nutrition counseling and psychobehavioral support, such as cognitive behavioral therapy, into prehabilitation may provide additional benefits, including reduced incidence of postoperative atrial fibrillation, improved mental health, and shorter recovery times. , , However, comprehensive, multimodal programs remain underused in cardiac surgery, and robust evidence from large randomized trials is still lacking. This review aims to provide a comprehensive evaluation of prehabilitation in the context of cardiac surgery. Specifically, we will (1) review the general concept of prehabilitation and its benefits, including evidence from other major surgery types, where such interventions have been more widely studied and implemented; (2) summarize references to prehabilitation in current national and international cardiac or other relevant surgical or perioperative guidelines; and (3) review existing studies for prehabilitation in cardiac surgery while identifying key opportunities, limitations, and gaps in the current evidence base. This synthesis will serve as a foundation for the development of future clinical trials aimed at evaluating prehabilitation as a standard component of perioperative care in cardiac surgery patients. In doing so, we aim to shift the paradigm from reactive recovery to proactive preparation, ultimately transforming how patients are supported before their hearts are ever touched. Methodology A systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE from inception to August 1, 2025, was performed using the Boolean string (“prehabilitation” OR “early rehabilitation”) AND (“cardiac” OR “cardiac surgery” OR “cardiovascular surgery”). This search yielded 325 publications, of which 43 full-text English-language articles were selected on the basis of relevance to prehabilitation only in cardiac surgery. One reviewer (S.K.P.) selected studies on the basis of these criteria and all authors evaluated them to ensure relevance. Supplementary PubMed/MEDLINE searches to contextualize findings across other surgical specialties were conducted pairing “prehabilitation” with thoracic surgery, oncology, vascular surgery, general surgery, and orthopedic/orthopaedic surgery. Prehabilitation Benefits in Noncardiac Surgery Major surgery imposes inflammatory and catabolic stress on patients; prehabilitation aims to address modifiable risks (eg, low aerobic fitness, malnutrition, respiratory muscle weakness, and adverse health behaviors) to improve physiologic reserve and self-management before the operation. , Across surgical populations, evidence shows the varied benefits of prehabilitation. In a meta-analysis of 178 randomized controlled trials (RCTs), the authors found that IMT, immunonutrition, and multimodal programs each shortened hospital stay by approximately 1.7 to 2.1 days. Exercise and IMT reduced postoperative pulmonary complications by 46% (risk ratio [RR], 0.54; 95% CI, 0.39-0.75) and 45% (RR, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.38-0.80), respectively. Immunonutrition and pre/probiotic therapy lowered infectious and wound complications by 36% (RR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.40-1.01) and 52% (RR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.14-1.62), respectively. Smoking cessation markedly reduced wound infection (RR, 0.28; 95% CI, 0.12-0.64). Mortality was unchanged, and the overall certainty of evidence was low. Contemporary reviews concur that multimodal regimens that combine exercise and nutrition outperform single-component exercise regimens. , Operationally, prehabilitation is feasible across candidate populations, including frail, high-risk patients, despite protocol heterogeneity. , Collectively, prehabilitation is a safe, pragmatic strategy that improves preoperative functional capacity and is associated with fewer pulmonary and infectious complications and shorter length of stay. The benefits of prehabilitation across other major noncardiac surgical specialties
